lessons.title: Lab: Parse CSV text into records

scenes.text: Asha receives a sales export pasted into an email as plain text.
Before any model, she must turn lines of text into typed records.

steps.title: Rows are strings
steps.body:
A CSV row is just a string. `line.split(',')` gives a list of strings; numbers must be converted with `int()` or `float()`.

The first line is usually the **header**; use it as dictionary keys so code reads `row['price']` instead of `row[2]`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert types, so `'3'+'4'` gives `'34'`.
- Splitting quoted fields that contain commas — use the `csv` module for real files.
- Leaving trailing newlines or spaces: use `.strip()`.

activity.prompt: Parse the CSV text and print the total revenue (qty × price summed).

raw = '''item,qty,price
pen,10,5.5
book,3,120
bag,2,450.25'''
lines = raw.strip().split('\n')
head = lines[0].split(',')
rows = [dict(zip(head, ln.split(','))) for ln in lines[1:]]
total = sum(int(r['qty']) * float(r['price']) for r in rows)
print(total)

scenes.text: A manager wants revenue per city, not per sale.

steps.title: The group-by pattern
steps.body: Group-by = **key → running total**. Loop over records; `totals[key] = totals.get(key, 0) + value`. `collections.defaultdict(float)` removes the `get`. `Counter` counts occurrences.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Sales: (Pune,100),(Delhi,50),(Pune,70). After loop: Pune = 170, Delhi = 50. Mean per city = total ÷ count: Pune 170/2 = **85**.

steps.title: Sorting results
steps.body: `sorted(d.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)` ranks groups by value. The `key` function says *what to compare*.

lessons.title: Lab: Comprehensions and missing values

scenes.text: A survey has blanks, 'NA' and impossible ages.

steps.title: Comprehensions
steps.body: `[f(x) for x in xs if cond]` builds a list; `{k: v for ...}` builds a dict; `{x for ...}` a set. They are faster to read and usually faster to run than append loops.

steps.title: Missing-value traps
steps.body:
- Never silently convert missing to 0; it drags the mean down.
- `None` is not `0` and not `''`.
- Decide and document: drop, impute (mean/median), or flag.

lessons.title: Lab: Pure functions for data cleaning

scenes.text: Ravi copy-pastes the same cleaning code in five notebooks.
He turns it into one tested function.

steps.title: What makes a function good
steps.body: A **pure function** returns a value from its inputs and changes nothing outside. It is easy to test (`assert f(2)==4`) and reuse. Give default arguments for options, and docstrings for intent.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: def zscore(xs): m = mean, s = std; return [(x-m)/s for x in xs]. For [2,4,6]: mean 4, population std = √(8/3)=1.633; z = [-1.22, 0, 1.22].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mutable default arguments (`def f(x, acc=[])`) are shared between calls.
- Modifying the input list in place surprises callers.
- Printing instead of returning.

activity.prompt: Write min_max(xs) returning values scaled to 0–1, and print the result for [10, 20, 40] rounded to 3 decimals.
activity.starter:
def min_max(xs):
    lo, hi = min(xs), max(xs)
    # TODO: scale each x
print([round(v, 3) for v in min_max([10, 20, 40])])
activity.solution:

    lo, hi = min(xs), max(xs)
    return [(x - lo) / (hi - lo) for x in xs]
print([round(v, 3) for v in min_max([10, 20, 40])])

lessons.title: Lab: Generators and lazy streams

scenes.text: A log is too big for memory.
A generator yields one line at a time.

steps.title: yield
steps.body: A function with `yield` returns a **generator**: values are produced lazily, one per `next()`. Memory use stays constant. Generator expressions: `(x*x for x in xs)`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: def evens(n): for i in range(n): if i%2==0: yield i. `sum(evens(10))` = 0+2+4+6+8 = **20**, without ever building a list.

steps.title: One-shot
steps.body: A generator can be consumed only once; recreate it or store with `list()` if you need two passes.

steps.title: Toolbox
steps.body: `zip(a, b)` pairs items; `enumerate` adds an index; `itertools.groupby` groups *consecutive* equal keys (sort first!); `Counter.most_common(n)` ranks; `itertools.combinations(xs, k)` lists k-subsets — there are C(n,k) of them.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Daily changes: prices [100,102,101,105] → [b-a for a,b in zip(p, p[1:])] = [2,-1,4]. combinations of 4 items taken 2 = 4!/(2!2!) = **6**.

steps.title: groupby trap
steps.body: `groupby` only merges adjacent keys; on unsorted data you get repeated groups.

lessons.title: Lab: Mean, median, mode and variance

scenes.text: Five salaries: four modest, one founder.
Mean and median disagree — why?

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Mean = Σx/n. Median = middle of the sorted list (average of two middles if n even). Sample variance s² = Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1); population σ² divides by n. Standard deviation = √variance.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: x = [4, 8, 6, 5, 7]: mean = 30/5 = 6. Deviations² = 4,4,0,1,1 → sum 10. Sample variance = 10/4 = **2.5**; population variance = 10/5 = 2. Sample sd = 1.581.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using n instead of n−1 for a sample.
- Reporting mean for skewed data (use median).
- Forgetting to sort before taking the median.

lessons.title: Lab: Percentiles, quartiles and outliers

scenes.text: A courier firm studies delivery minutes.
Outliers are flagged with the 1.5×IQR rule.

steps.title: Quartiles and IQR
steps.body: Q1, Q2, Q3 split sorted data in quarters; IQR = Q3 − Q1. The Tukey fences are Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR; points beyond are flagged as outliers. With linear interpolation the p-th percentile sits at position (n−1)·p/100 (0-indexed).

steps.title: Libraries differ
steps.body: There are several percentile definitions; always check which method (e.g. linear) your tool uses.

    s = sorted(xs)
    pos = (len(s) - 1) * p / 100
    lo = int(pos)
    hi = min(lo + 1, len(s) - 1)
    # TODO: interpolate
x = [10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 18, 20, 45]
q1, q3 = pct(x, 25), pct(x, 75)
iqr = q3 - q1
out = [v for v in x if v < q1 - 1.5 * iqr or v > q3 + 1.5 * iqr]
print(q1, q3, out)
activity.solution:
def pct(xs, p):
    s = sorted(xs)
    pos = (len(s) - 1) * p / 100
    lo = int(pos)
    hi = min(lo + 1, len(s) - 1)
    return s[lo] + (s[hi] - s[lo]) * (pos - lo)
x = [10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 18, 20, 45]
q1, q3 = pct(x, 25), pct(x, 75)
iqr = q3 - q1
out = [v for v in x if v < q1 - 1.5 * iqr or v > q3 + 1.5 * iqr]
print(q1, q3, out)

lessons.title: Lab: Correlation and z-scores

scenes.text: Hours studied vs marks for six students.
Pearson r measures the linear link.

steps.title: Pearson r
steps.body: r = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / √(Σ(x−x̄)² · Σ(y−ȳ)²). It lies in [−1, 1]. z-score: z = (x−μ)/σ tells how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.

steps.title: Correlation ≠ causation
steps.body: A strong r can come from a lurking variable or coincidence; r only captures linear association and is sensitive to outliers.

    num = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
    # TODO: denominator
    return num / den

activity.solution:
from math import sqrt
def pearson(x, y):
    mx, my = sum(x) / len(x), sum(y) / len(y)
    num = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
    den = sqrt(sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x) * sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in y))
    return num / den
print(round(pearson([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [2, 4, 5, 4, 5]), 3))

from math import sqrt
def summary(xs):
    n = len(xs)
    m = sum(xs) / n
    s = sorted(xs)
    med = (s[n//2 - 1] + s[n//2]) / 2 if n % 2 == 0 else s[n//2]
    sd = sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / (n - 1))
    return n, round(m, 2), med, round(sd, 2)
print(summary([56, 67, 72, 72, 85, 90]))

steps.title: Normalisation
steps.body: Typical steps: `strip()`, `lower()`, collapse whitespace with `' '.join(s.split())`, remove punctuation, standardise accents. Then use a **set** to deduplicate.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ['  RAVI kumar','ravi  Kumar','Ravi Kumar','Asha Rao'] → normalised {'ravi kumar','asha rao'} → **2** unique people.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Lowercasing keys *after* comparing them.
- Using `str.replace` for patterns that need regex.
- Forgetting that strings are immutable — methods return new strings.

lessons.title: Lab: Regular expressions for extraction

scenes.text: Hundreds of emails hide invoice numbers and amounts.

steps.title: Core syntax
steps.body: `\d` digit, `\w` word char, `+` one or more, `*` zero or more, `?` optional, `[A-Z]` class, `(...)` capture group, `^`/`$` anchors. `re.findall(pattern, text)` returns all matches (groups if present).

steps.title: Raw strings
steps.body: Write patterns as raw strings `r'\d+'` to avoid double backslashes.

lessons.title: Lab: Flattening nested JSON

scenes.text: A shop API returns orders with nested customer and items.
Analysts need a flat table.

steps.title: json module
steps.body: `json.loads(text)` converts JSON to dicts/lists; `json.dumps` goes back. Nested data → flat rows by looping over the inner list and copying outer fields (one row per item = **exploding**).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Order o1 (customer Asha) has items qty 2 @ 50 and qty 1 @ 30. Flat rows: (o1, Asha, 2, 50), (o1, Asha, 1, 30). Order value = 2×50 + 30 = **130**.

steps.title: Pitfalls
steps.body:
- Missing keys: use `.get`.
- JSON has no tuples or NaN by standard; `null` becomes `None`.

steps.title: Seeds
steps.body: Pseudo-random generators are deterministic given a seed. `random.seed(42)` or a local `rng = random.Random(42)` makes shuffles and samples repeat. Use a *local* generator in functions so other code cannot disturb it. Report the seed.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Shuffle indices 0..9 with seed 0 twice → identical orders. A 80/20 split of 10 items gives 8 train and **2** test items.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- Seeding once at the top then relying on call order.
- Reporting one lucky seed instead of the mean over several seeds.

scenes.text: A lookup inside a loop scans a list each time.

steps.title: Big-O in practice
steps.body: Membership test: list O(n), set/dict O(1) average. Nested loops O(n²). Sorting O(n log n). `time.perf_counter()` measures elapsed time; compare approaches on the same data, run a few times.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Checking 1,000 queries against a 1,000-item list ≈ 1,000×1,000 = 1,000,000 comparisons worst-case; against a set ≈ 1,000 lookups — roughly **1000× fewer** steps.

steps.title: Premature optimisation
steps.body: Measure first. Clarity beats cleverness unless the profiler shows a hotspot.

lessons.title: Lab: Stationarity, differencing and ACF

story.title: Does the past predict the present?

scenes.text: A random walk wanders; its changes do not.
Autocorrelation reveals memory.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: A **stationary** series has constant mean, variance and autocovariance over time. First difference Δyₜ = yₜ − yₜ₋₁ removes a stochastic trend. ACF at lag k: rₖ = Σ(yₜ−ȳ)(yₜ₊ₖ−ȳ)/Σ(yₜ−ȳ)². For white noise rₖ ≈ 0, with 95% bounds ±1.96/√n.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: n=100 → bounds ±0.196: ACF values inside them are not significant.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Differencing too much adds spurious negative autocorrelation.

activity.prompt: Difference the series and compute ACF lags 1–3 of the differenced series (3 d.p.).
activity.starter:

m = sum(d) / len(d)
den = sum((v - m) ** 2 for v in d)
# TODO: autocorrelation at lag k
print(d)
print([round(acf(k), 3) for k in (1, 2, 3)])
activity.solution:
y = [10, 12, 15, 14, 18, 21, 20, 25, 27, 26, 31, 34]
d = [b - a for a, b in zip(y, y[1:])]
m = sum(d) / len(d)
den = sum((v - m) ** 2 for v in d)
acf = lambda k: sum((d[i] - m) * (d[i + k] - m) for i in range(len(d) - k)) / den
print(d)
print([round(acf(k), 3) for k in (1, 2, 3)])

lessons.title: Lab: Fit an AR(1) model

scenes.text: Daily temperature anomalies persist.
Estimate φ by least squares.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: yₜ = c + φyₜ₋₁ + εₜ. Stationary if |φ| < 1. Regress yₜ on yₜ₋₁ (simple regression). Forecast h steps: ŷ = μ + φʰ(yₜ − μ) where μ = c/(1−φ) — forecasts decay to the mean.

steps.title: Half-life
steps.body: Shock half-life = ln 0.5/ln φ ≈ 3.1 steps for φ=0.8.

lessons.title: Lab: Residual diagnostics and anomaly detection

scenes.text: If residuals still have structure, the model missed something.

steps.title: Checks
steps.body: Residuals should be uncorrelated (ACF within bounds), mean ≈ 0, constant variance. Ljung–Box test pools autocorrelations: Q = n(n+2)Σ rₖ²/(n−k). Anomalies: |z| > 3 for rolling mean/sd (computed on past data only).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Rolling window 5: values mean 10, sd 1; a new value 15 → z = 5 → anomaly. Masking: if an earlier spike is still inside the window, the sd inflates and a second spike can slip through (see the code output).

lessons.title: Lab: Population Stability Index

scenes.text: Average age of applicants has crept up.
PSI quantifies the shift.

steps.title: PSI
steps.body: Bin the training (expected) distribution; PSI = Σ (aᵢ − eᵢ) ln(aᵢ/eᵢ) where aᵢ, eᵢ are the fractions per bin. Rule of thumb: <0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate shift, >0.25 major shift.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Empty bins → ln 0; add a small epsilon.

lessons.title: Lab: Kolmogorov–Smirnov drift test

scenes.text: Is this week's transaction amount distribution the same as training?
KS measures the largest CDF gap.

steps.title: KS statistic
steps.body: D = max over x of |F₁(x) − F₂(x)|. Large D → distributions differ. Critical value (α=0.05) ≈ 1.36·√((n+m)/(nm)).

steps.title: Many features
steps.body: Testing 100 features at α=0.05 gives ~5 false alarms; correct for multiple tests or alert on the share drifting.

lessons.title: Lab: Compute group fairness metrics

scenes.text: A bank approves 60% of group A but 40% of group B.
Measure the gaps.

steps.title: Metrics
steps.body: **Demographic parity**: equal selection rate P(Ŷ=1|G). **Disparate impact ratio** = rate_B/rate_A (the US '80% rule' flags <0.8 as potential adverse impact). **Equal opportunity**: equal TPR across groups. **Equalised odds**: equal TPR and FPR. **Predictive parity**: equal precision.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Selection rates 0.40 vs 0.60 → ratio 0.667 < 0.8 → flag. TPR_A=0.80, TPR_B=0.60 → equal-opportunity gap 0.20.

steps.title: Not legal advice
steps.body: Legal thresholds differ by jurisdiction; treat the 80% rule as a screening heuristic.

lessons.title: Lab: Trade-offs and mitigation

scenes.text: Groups have different base rates.
Choose what to equalise — and say why.

steps.title: Impossibility
steps.body: When base rates differ between groups, a non-perfect classifier cannot satisfy calibration/predictive parity and equal FPR/FNR simultaneously (Kleinberg et al.; Chouldechova 2017). So fairness is a value decision, documented with stakeholders. Mitigation: pre-processing (reweighing), in-processing (constraints), post-processing (group-specific thresholds).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Reweighing weight for (group g, label y) = P(g)P(y)/P(g,y). If P(B)=0.4, P(y=1)=0.3, P(B,y=1)=0.08 → weight = 0.4·0.3/0.08 = **1.5** (upweight underrepresented positives).

lessons.title: Lab: k-anonymity and re-identification

scenes.text: Zip code, birth year and gender uniquely identify many people.
Linking datasets re-identifies them.

steps.title: k-anonymity
steps.body: A table is k-anonymous if every combination of quasi-identifiers appears in at least k rows. Achieve by generalising (age 34 → 30–39, zip 560034 → 5600**) and suppressing rare rows. Limits: homogeneity attacks (all rows in a group share the same sensitive value) → l-diversity.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Groups (30–39,5600**): 3 rows; (40–49,5600**): 1 row → table is only **1-anonymous** (min group size 1).

steps.title: India
steps.body: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets purpose limitation, consent and data-principal rights for personal data processing in India; this is general education, not legal advice.

lessons.title: Lab: Differential privacy with the Laplace mechanism

scenes.text: Publish the number of patients with a rare condition without exposing any individual.
Add calibrated noise.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A mechanism M is ε-differentially private if for any two datasets differing in one person, P(M(D)∈S) ≤ e^ε P(M(D′)∈S). For a count (sensitivity 1) add Laplace noise with scale b = 1/ε. Smaller ε → stronger privacy, more noise. Noise standard deviation = √2·b.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ε=0.5 → b=2 → sd = 2.83. ε=0.1 → b=10 → sd = 14.1. Privacy budgets add up over repeated queries (composition).

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Answering unlimited queries with fresh noise lets an attacker average the noise away.

activity.prompt: Compute Laplace scale and noise standard deviation for ε = 1, 0.5, 0.1 (sensitivity 1) and the probability bound e^ε (3 d.p.).
activity.starter:

for eps in (1, 0.5, 0.1):
    # TODO: scale for sensitivity 1

activity.solution:
from math import exp, sqrt
for eps in (1, 0.5, 0.1):
    b = 1 / eps
    print(eps, b, round(sqrt(2) * b, 3), round(exp(eps), 3))

lessons.title: Lab: Permutation importance and Shapley values

story.title: Why did the model say no?

scenes.text: A customer asks why their loan was declined.
Explain with global and local methods.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: **Permutation importance**: shuffle one feature; importance = drop in score. **Shapley value** of feature i = average marginal contribution over all orderings (exact for few features). Local explanations support individual decisions; global ones support auditing.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Model f(x₁,x₂) = 3x₁ + 2x₂ + x₁x₂, baseline (0,0), instance (1,1): f=6. Shapley φ₁ = ½[(f(1,0)−f(0,0)) + (f(1,1)−f(0,1))] = ½[3 + 4] = **3.5**; φ₂ = ½[2 + 3] = 2.5; sum = 6 ✓ (efficiency).

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: Correlated features make permutation importance misleading; explanations describe the model, not causes in the world.

s = [(sum((r[i] - m[i]) ** 2 for r in tr) / len(tr)) ** 0.5 for i in range(2)]
Z = lambda r: [(r[i] - m[i]) / s[i] for i in range(2)]
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
w, b = [0.0, 0.0], 0.0
for _ in range(800):
    gw, gb = [0.0, 0.0], 0.0
    for r in tr:
        z = Z(r)
        e = sig(w[0] * z[0] + w[1] * z[1] + b) - r[2]
        gw = [gw[0] + e * z[0], gw[1] + e * z[1]]
        gb += e
    w = [w[i] - 0.5 * gw[i] / len(tr) for i in range(2)]
    b -= 0.5 * gb / len(tr)
P = [sig(sum(wi * zi for wi, zi in zip(w, Z(r))) + b) for r in va]
acc = sum((p >= 0.5) == r[2] for p, r in zip(P, va)) / len(va)
ll = -sum(r[2] * log(p) + (1 - r[2]) * log(1 - p) for p, r in zip(P, va)) / len(va)
print(round(acc, 3), round(ll, 3))

lessons.title: What an ERP is and how SAP structures a company

scenes.text: At Contoso Foods, Sales keeps orders in one sheet, the warehouse keeps stock in another, and Finance keeps invoices in a third.
On month-end the three totals disagree and nobody knows which one is right.
The CFO approves an ERP project: one database, one version of the truth, shared by every department.

steps.title: ERP in one paragraph
steps.body: An **ERP** (Enterprise Resource Planning) system runs the core processes of a company on **one integrated database**: finance, purchasing, inventory, sales, production, HR. When the warehouse posts a goods receipt, the stock quantity, the inventory value in the books and the vendor liability all update from that single event.

steps.title: Organisational units you must know
steps.body:
- **Client**: the highest level, a self-contained unit with its own master data (usually one per system environment, e.g. client 100).
- **Company code**: the smallest unit for which a full legal set of books can be produced (one legal entity).
- **Plant**: a location that produces or stores goods (logistics).
- **Storage location**: a place inside a plant where stock is kept.
- **Purchasing organisation / sales organisation**: who buys, who sells.

steps.title: Finance building blocks
steps.body:
- **Chart of accounts**: the list of G/L accounts; assigned to company codes.
- **Fiscal year variant**: defines posting periods (e.g. April–March for India).
- **Posting key / document type**: tell the system debit or credit and the kind of document (e.g. vendor invoice).
- Every posting creates an **accounting document** where **total debits = total credits**.

steps.title: Worked example · a balanced document
steps.body:
Office rent of 40,000 plus 18% GST input tax is paid by bank.
- Rent expense debit: 40,000
- GST input tax debit: 40,000 × 0.18 = 7,200
- Bank credit: 40,000 + 7,200 = **47,200**

Debits 47,200 = credits 47,200, so the document can be posted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing **client** with **company code**: one client can hold many company codes.
- Thinking the ERP replaces process discipline; wrong master data produces wrong results quickly.
- Forgetting that a posting period must be open for the date you post.

lessons.title: The shell, the prompt and command anatomy

scenes.text: Arjun joins a hosting company in Pune. His lead gives him a login to dev01.contoso.local.
He sees [arjun@dev01 ~]$ and a blinking cursor. Where is he, who is he, and what can he type?

steps.title: What a shell is
steps.body:
The **shell** (usually **bash**) is a program that reads a line you type, expands it (variables, wildcards, quotes) and starts other programs.

- `[arjun@dev01 ~]$` = user **arjun**, host **dev01**, current directory **~** (home), `$` = normal user (`#` = root).
- Command anatomy: `command -options arguments`, e.g. `ls -l /etc`.
- Short options combine: `ls -la` = `ls -l -a`. Long options use two dashes: `ls --all`.

steps.title: Solved example: reading a command
steps.body:
`cp -rv /etc/nginx /root/nginx-backup`

- `cp` = command (copy)
- `-r` = recursive (directories), `-v` = verbose
- `/etc/nginx` = source, `/root/nginx-backup` = destination.

Second example: `tail -n 20 /var/log/messages` prints the last 20 lines of the system log.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Linux is **case-sensitive**: `Documents` ≠ `documents`.
- Spaces separate arguments: `cd My Files` tries to go to `My`. Quote it: `cd "My Files"`.
- Do not work as root for everyday tasks; use `sudo` only when needed.

lessons.title: Lab: Navigate the filesystem hierarchy

scenes.text: Arjun's lead asks: 'Find the nginx config and the nginx logs, then come back home.'
He needs to understand the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS).

steps.title: The FHS map
steps.body:
- `/` root of everything (one tree, even with many disks)
- `/etc` system configuration (text files)
- `/var` variable data: `/var/log` logs, `/var/lib` databases, `/var/spool` queues
- `/home` users' homes; `/root` root's home
- `/usr` installed programs and libraries (`/usr/bin`, `/usr/lib`)
- `/tmp` temporary files (often cleaned at boot)
- `/proc`, `/sys` virtual files exposing kernel state
- `/dev` device files (`/dev/sda`, `/dev/null`)
- `/boot` kernel and bootloader files

steps.title: Absolute vs relative paths
steps.body:
Absolute starts at `/`: `/var/log/nginx`.
Relative starts where you are: if you are in `/var`, then `log/nginx` is the same place.

- `.` = current dir, `..` = parent, `~` = home, `cd -` = previous dir.

Example: from `/etc/nginx/conf.d`, `cd ../..` lands in `/etc`.

steps.title: Always check where you are
steps.body: `pwd` prints the working directory. Run it before any `rm`.

activity.prompt: You are arjun on dev01. Print your current directory, go to the nginx configuration directory, list it, then visit the nginx log directory and return home.

scenes.text: Arjun must set up /home/arjun/reports/2026 with monthly folders and archive old drafts.

steps.title: Core file commands
steps.body:
- `mkdir -p a/b/c` makes parents as needed
- `touch f` creates an empty file or updates its timestamp
- `cp src dst`, `cp -r dir dst`, `cp -a` (archive: keep permissions, times, links)
- `mv old new` renames or moves
- `rm file`, `rm -r dir`, `rmdir emptydir`
- `rm -i` asks before each delete

steps.title: Solved example: brace expansion
steps.body:
`mkdir -p reports/2026/{01..03}` creates `reports/2026/01`, `02`, `03` in one go.

`cp notes.txt{,.bak}` expands to `cp notes.txt notes.txt.bak` — a quick backup.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `rm -rf / tmp/x` (stray space) is catastrophic. Read the line twice.
- `mv a b` silently overwrites `b`; use `mv -i` or `-n`.
- `cp dir dst` without `-r` fails: 'omitting directory'.

lessons.title: Lab: Links, inodes, globbing and find

scenes.text: Two files show the same content and editing one changes the other. A colleague says: 'It's a hard link.'
Then Arjun needs every .log over 100 MB on the box — find to the rescue.

steps.title: Inodes and links
steps.body:
Each file's metadata (owner, mode, size, block pointers) lives in an **inode**; a directory entry maps a name to an inode number (`ls -i`).

- **Hard link** `ln a b`: a second name for the same inode; same filesystem only; file survives until the last link is removed.
- **Symbolic link** `ln -s target name`: a small file containing a path; can cross filesystems; breaks if the target moves.

steps.title: Globbing and find
steps.body:
Globs are expanded by the shell: `*.log`, `file?.txt`, `[abc]*`.

`find /var -name '*.log' -size +100M` — files over 100 MiB.
`find /tmp -type f -mtime +7 -delete` — delete files modified more than 7 days ago.
`find / -user arjun 2>/dev/null` — files owned by arjun, errors hidden.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quote patterns for find (`-name '*.log'`) or the shell expands them first.
- Test `find … -print` before adding `-delete`.

Can point to a directory on another disk
Is another name for the same inode

quiz.why: Hard links share the inode; data stays until the link count is 0.
Inode numbers are only unique within one filesystem.

options: So the shell doesn't expand it before find sees it

lessons.title: Streams, redirection and pipes

scenes.text: A cron job emails root 400 messages a day because its errors aren't redirected.

steps.title: Three standard streams
steps.body:
- 0 stdin, 1 stdout, 2 stderr
- `>` overwrite stdout to file, `>>` append
- `2>` stderr, `&>` or `>file 2>&1` both
- `<` feed a file as stdin
- `|` connects stdout of one command to stdin of the next
- `tee file` writes to a file AND passes data on

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. `backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1` — append both streams.
2. `dnf list installed | wc -l` — count installed package lines.
3. `df -h | tee /tmp/df.txt` — see output and save it.

steps.title: Order matters
steps.body: `cmd 2>&1 > file` sends stderr to the *terminal* (where stdout pointed at that moment) and only stdout to file. Write `cmd > file 2>&1`.

activity.prompt: Match each operator to its effect
pairs: Copy stream to file and screen

quiz.q: Which captures both stdout and stderr into out.log?
quiz.why: Redirect stdout first, then dup stderr onto it.

lessons.title: Lab: grep and regular expressions on real logs

scenes.text: The security team asks Meera which IPs had failed SSH logins on bastion01 today.
/var/log/secure has 80,000 lines. grep makes it 5 seconds.

steps.title: grep essentials
steps.body:
- `grep -i` ignore case, `-v` invert, `-n` line numbers, `-c` count, `-r` recursive, `-l` file names only
- `-E` extended regex: `+ ? | ()` without backslashes
- `-o` print only the matching part
- Anchors `^` start, `$` end; `.` any char; `[0-9]` class; `{1,3}` repetition

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
`grep 'Failed password' /var/log/secure | grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`

Result: a ranked list of attacking IPs. Second example: `grep -v '^#' /etc/ssh/sshd_config | grep -v '^$'` shows only active settings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `-E` so `+` is literal in basic regex.
- `grep error` misses `ERROR`; use `-i`.

steps.title: sed basics
steps.body:
- `sed 's/old/new/' f` replace first match per line, `s/old/new/g` all
- `-i` edit in place, `-i.bak` keep a backup
- `-n '5,10p'` print lines 5–10
- `/pattern/d` delete matching lines
- Any delimiter: `s|/usr/local|/opt|g`

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. `sed -i.bak 's/^#\?PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config` — handles commented or uncommented line.
2. `sed -n '/\[mysqld\]/,/^\[/p' /etc/my.cnf` — print the [mysqld] section.

steps.title: Validate before reload

scenes.text: The product owner asks: top 5 URLs by hits and the count of 5xx errors in today's nginx log.

steps.title: awk in one screen
steps.body:
`awk 'pattern { action }' file`. Fields split on whitespace by default; `-F:` sets the separator.

- `$0` whole line, `$1`… fields, `NF` field count, `NR` line number
- `awk -F: '$3>=1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd` — human users
- `awk '{s+=$10} END {print s}'` — sum a column

steps.title: Solved example: nginx combined log
steps.body:
Combined format fields: $1 client IP, $7 request path, $9 status, $10 bytes.

- Top URLs: `awk '{print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5`
- 5xx count: `awk '$9 ~ /^5/' access.log | wc -l`
- `cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd` user and shell

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using single quotes outside and `$7` inside is correct; double quotes let bash expand `$7` to an empty string first.

lessons.title: Reading ls -l and the rwx model

scenes.text: Kavya in Finance says she can see report.xlsx on the share but 'Permission denied' when opening it.
ls -l tells the whole story in ten characters.

steps.title: Ten characters
steps.body:
`-rw-r----- 1 ravi finance 8192 Nov 26 report.xlsx`

- 1st char: type (`-` file, `d` dir, `l` link)
- Then three triplets: **user (owner)**, **group**, **others**
- r=4, w=2, x=1 → rw-r----- = **640**

steps.title: On directories it's different
steps.body:
- **r** list names
- **w** create, delete, rename entries (needs x too)
- **x** enter/traverse (`cd`, access files inside)

So deleting a file depends on the *directory's* w, not the file's.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. `rwxr-x---` = 7,5,0 = **750**.
2. 644 = rw-r--r--: owner edits, everyone reads.
3. Kavya is not ravi and not in group finance → 'others' = --- → denied.

activity.prompt: Which permission (on a DIRECTORY) is needed for each action?

options: w and x on the containing directory

lessons.title: Lab: chmod, chown and chgrp

scenes.text: The deploy user must own /srv/app; the web group must read it; nobody else should see it.

steps.title: Commands
steps.body:

- `chgrp web file`
- `chmod 750 dir`, `chmod u+x script.sh`, `chmod g-w,o= file`
- `chmod -R u=rwX,g=rX,o= /srv/app` — capital X: execute only on directories (or already-executable files)

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Goal: dirs 750, files 640 under /srv/app.
`find /srv/app -type d -exec chmod 750 {} +` and `find /srv/app -type f -exec chmod 640 {} +`.

lessons.title: Lab: umask and special bits

scenes.text: New log files from an app are created world-readable and contain customer emails.
The culprit is the service's umask of 0022.

steps.title: umask
steps.body:
New files start from 666, directories from 777; the umask bits are **removed**.

- umask 022 → files 644, dirs 755
- umask 027 → files 640, dirs 750
- umask 077 → files 600, dirs 700

Set per shell with `umask 027`, per systemd service with `UMask=0027`.

steps.title: setuid, setgid, sticky
steps.body:
- **setuid (4)** on an executable: runs as file owner (`/usr/bin/passwd` → `-rwsr-xr-x`)
- **setgid (2)** on a directory: new files inherit the directory's group
- **sticky (1)** on a directory: only owner can delete their files (`/tmp` → `drwxrwxrwt`)

`chmod 2770 /srv/shared` = setgid + rwxrwx---.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: umask 027, new dir: 777 − 027 → 750. New file: 666 with 027 masked → 640 (umask removes bits; it is not plain subtraction, e.g. 666 with umask 033 → 644).

activity.prompt: A service runs with umask 0077. What octal mode will a newly created regular file get? (enter 3 digits)

quiz.q: With umask 022, a new directory gets…

options: New files to inherit the directory's group

scenes.text: An external auditor, user audit1, needs read access to /srv/finance — but must not be added to the finance group.

steps.title: ACL commands
steps.body:
- `setfacl -m u:audit1:rX /srv/finance` grant
- `setfacl -R -m u:audit1:rX /srv/finance` existing contents
- `setfacl -d -m u:audit1:rX /srv/finance` **default** ACL for future files
- `getfacl /srv/finance` view; `setfacl -x u:audit1` remove one; `setfacl -b` remove all
- `ls -l` shows a `+` after the mode when an ACL exists

steps.title: The mask
steps.body: The ACL **mask** caps group-class entries (named users, named groups, owning group). If mask is `r--`, a named user given `rwx` is effectively `r--`. chmod on the group bits changes the mask.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the default ACL so new files are invisible to the auditor.
- Copying with tools that don't preserve ACLs (use `cp -a`, `rsync -A`).

lessons.title: Identity files: passwd, shadow, group

scenes.text: A file is owned by 1003 and no name shows. Neha has to find out what happened.
The account was deleted but its files were left behind.

steps.title: /etc/passwd (7 fields)
steps.body:
`neha:x:1001:1001:Neha Iyer:/home/neha:/bin/bash`

name : x(password in shadow) : UID : primary GID : comment (GECOS) : home : shell.

UID 0 = root; system accounts usually < 1000 on RHEL/Debian-family.

steps.title: /etc/shadow and /etc/group
steps.body:

courses.summary: What a process is, how to see it (ps, top, pgrep, /proc), job control, the signals you will actually use, nice/renice, and dealing with zombies and runaway processes. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can inspect processes with ps, pgrep and /proc

lessons.title: Processes, PIDs and states

scenes.text: On app02 the fan screams. Imran opens a terminal.
Every running program is a process with a PID, a parent, a state and an owner.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **PID** unique id, **PPID** parent; PID 1 is systemd
- States: **R** running/runnable, **S** interruptible sleep, **D** uninterruptible sleep (usually I/O), **T** stopped, **Z** zombie (exited, parent hasn't reaped)
- `ps aux` BSD style, `ps -ef` System V style, `ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,%cpu,%mem,cmd --sort=-%cpu | head`

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. `pgrep -a java` → `4412 /usr/bin/java -jar billing.jar`.
2. `cat /proc/4412/status | grep -E 'State|VmRSS'` → State: S (sleeping), VmRSS: 812344 kB.
3. `pstree -p 1 | head` shows the tree.

steps.title: Zombies
steps.body: You cannot kill a zombie — it's already dead. Fix or restart its **parent** so it reaps the child (or the zombie is adopted and reaped when the parent exits).

activity.prompt: Match the ps STAT letter to the meaning

quiz.q: How do you get rid of many zombies?
quiz.why: Zombies are reaped by the parent.

quiz.q: A process in D state is usually…
options: Waiting on I/O and can't be interrupted

lessons.title: Lab: Signals and killing processes correctly

scenes.text: A reporting job has hung for 3 hours holding a lock.

steps.title: Signals you'll use
steps.body:
- **SIGTERM (15)** default of kill: please exit cleanly
- **SIGKILL (9)** immediate, can't be caught; no cleanup
- **SIGHUP (1)** many daemons reload config
- **SIGINT (2)** Ctrl+C
- **SIGSTOP (19)/SIGCONT (18)** pause/resume (numbers on x86 Linux)

`kill PID`, `kill -9 PID`, `pkill -u user`, `killall name`

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `pgrep -f report.py` → 7781. `kill 7781`; wait 10 s; `ps -p 7781` still present → `kill -9 7781`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting with -9 leaves temp files, locks and half-written data.
- `pkill -f java` may match more than you think — check with `pgrep -af java` first.

steps.title: Job control
steps.body:
- `cmd &` start in background
- Ctrl+Z suspend foreground job
- `jobs`, `fg %1`, `bg %1`
- `nohup cmd > out.log 2>&1 &` ignore hangup when you log out
- `disown %1` remove from the shell's job table
- Better for long work: `tmux`/`screen` sessions you can reattach

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `rsync -a /data/ backup01:/data/` running → Ctrl+Z → `bg` → `disown -h %1`. Now logging out won't kill it.

steps.title: Long-running = service
steps.body: If something must always run, make it a systemd unit, not a nohup job.

lessons.title: Lab: Priorities with nice and renice

scenes.text: The nightly compression job makes the web API slow.

steps.title: Niceness
steps.body:
Nice values range **−20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest)**; default 0.

- `nice -n 10 tar czf …` start lower priority
- `renice -n 15 -p PID` change running process
- Only root can lower niceness (raise priority)
- `ionice -c3 cmd` idle I/O class for disk-heavy jobs

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `ps -o pid,ni,cmd -p 9120` → NI 0. `renice -n 15 -p 9120` → '9120 (process ID) old priority 0, new priority 15'.

steps.title: Nice ≠ limit
steps.body: Nice only matters when the CPU is contended. To cap resources use systemd `CPUQuota=` / cgroups.

lessons.title: Lab: Your first script, variables and quoting

scenes.text: Every morning Leela pastes the same five health commands. Time to script it.
She learns that quoting mistakes are the #1 source of script bugs.

steps.title: Anatomy
steps.body:
```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
name="web01"   # no spaces around =
echo "Host: $name"
```
- `chmod +x health.sh` then `./health.sh`
- `set -e` exit on error, `-u` error on unset vars, `-o pipefail` pipeline fails if any part fails

steps.title: Quoting rules
steps.body:
- Double quotes: expand `$var` and `$(cmd)` but keep spaces → **always quote variables**: `"$file"`
- Single quotes: literal
- Command substitution: `today=$(date +%F)`

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `file="My Report.txt"; rm $file` tries to remove `My` and `Report.txt`. `rm "$file"` removes the right file.

lessons.title: Lab: Conditions, tests and exit codes

scenes.text: Leela wants the script to warn only when / is above 85%.
Conditions and exit codes make scripts decide.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body:
- `[[ -f $f ]]` file exists, `-d` dir, `-r` readable, `-z "$s"` empty string
- Numbers: `-gt -lt -ge -le -eq -ne` or `(( n > 85 ))`
- Strings: `==`, `!=`, `=~` regex in `[[ ]]`
- `$?` exit code of last command: 0 = success
- `cmd && echo ok || echo fail`

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
```
use=$(df --output=pcent / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9')
if (( use > 85 )); then
  echo "WARN: / at ${use}%"; exit 1
fi
echo "OK: / at ${use}%"
```

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: `[ $a == $b ]` breaks when a is empty. Use `[[ "$a" == "$b" ]]`. Use exit codes for monitoring tools: 0 OK, non-zero problem.

steps.title: Functions & traps
steps.body:
```
log() { echo "$(date '+%F %T') $*" | tee -a /var/log/myjob.log; }
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
```
- `local var` inside functions
- `return n` sets the function's exit code
- `logger -t myjob "msg"` writes to syslog/journal

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `trap 'log "failed at line $LINENO"' ERR` reports where a strict-mode script died.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using fixed names like /tmp/work allows races and symlink attacks; use mktemp.

Do the work, logging each step

steps.title: Requirements
steps.body:

- Strict mode, logging, trap cleanup
- find files `*.log -mtime +7`

steps.title: Core lines
steps.body:
```
mapfile -t files < <(find "$dir" -name '*.log' -mtime +7)
(( ${#files[@]} )) || { log 'nothing to do'; exit 0; }
tar czf "$out" "${files[@]}" && tar tzf "$out" >/dev/null && rm -f "${files[@]}"
```

steps.title: Verify before delete
steps.body: `tar tzf` reads the archive back — never delete originals before verifying.

lessons.title: How DNS resolution works

steps.title: Flow
steps.body: App → stub resolver (glibc, nsswitch) → configured resolver (e.g. 10.20.0.10 or systemd-resolved 127.0.0.53) → recursive lookup: root → TLD (.local is special; use real zones in production) → authoritative server → answer cached for TTL

steps.title: Records
steps.body:
- A / AAAA: IPv4 / IPv6
- CNAME: alias
- MX: mail servers (priority)
- TXT: SPF, verification
- NS: delegation; SOA: zone metadata (serial, refresh, negative TTL)
- PTR: reverse lookup

steps.title: TTL
steps.body: TTL 3600 → resolvers may serve the old IP for up to an hour after a change. Lower it days before migrations.

courses.title: TLS certificates: CSRs, renewals & expiry
courses.summary: Certificates without fear: keys, CSRs, chains and SANs, configuring TLS in nginx, ACME automation with certbot, monitoring expiry and handling the classic expired-certificate outage. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.

lessons.title: PKI in one lesson

scenes.text: Junior admin Pia is asked to 'renew the cert' and doesn't know where to start.
Keys, CSRs, CAs and chains.

steps.title: Pieces
steps.body:
- **Private key** stays on the server (mode 600)
- **CSR** (certificate signing request) = public key + names, signed by the key
- **CA** verifies and issues the **certificate** (public key + names + validity + CA signature)
- **Chain**: leaf → intermediate(s) → root (root trusted by clients)
- **SAN** (Subject Alternative Name) is what browsers check — CN alone isn't enough

steps.title: Lifetimes
steps.body: Under the CA/Browser Forum schedule, the maximum lifetime of publicly trusted TLS certificates dropped from 398 to 200 days in March 2026, and is scheduled to fall to 100 days (2027) and 47 days (2029). Internal-CA certificates follow your own policy. Either way, automation is essential.

steps.title: Never email private keys
steps.body: If a key leaks, revoke and reissue.

steps.title: certbot
steps.body:
- `certbot --nginx -d status.example.com` obtain + configure
- `certbot certonly --webroot -w /srv/status -d status.example.com` obtain only
- Renewal via systemd timer (`certbot-renew.timer` / `certbot.timer`) or cron; `certbot renew --dry-run`
- Deploy hook: `--deploy-hook 'systemctl reload nginx'`
- `certbot certificates` lists expiry dates
- HTTP-01 needs port 80 reachable; DNS-01 for wildcards/internal

steps.title: Let's Encrypt lifetime
steps.body: Let's Encrypt certificates are short-lived (90 days at the time of writing); certbot renews when roughly 30 days remain.

courses.title: Performance troubleshooting: CPU, memory, disk
courses.summary: A senior admin's method for 'the server is slow': USE method, load average, top/htop, vmstat, iostat, sar, free and the page cache, OOM killer, iowait and disk latency, with real output interpretation. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can apply the USE method to CPU, memory, disk and network
Learners can read top, vmstat, iostat and free correctly
Learners can distinguish CPU-bound, memory-bound and I/O-bound load
Learners can use sar history to explain past incidents

lessons.title: The USE method and load average

scenes.text: Three vague tickets a day say 'slow'. Senior admin Vikas teaches a method.
Utilisation, Saturation, Errors — for every resource.

steps.title: USE
steps.body:
For each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network):
- **Utilisation** — how busy (CPU %, disk %util)
- **Saturation** — queued work (run queue, swap activity, disk queue/await)
- **Errors** — (dmesg, NIC errors, disk errors)

steps.title: Load average
steps.body:
1/5/15-minute averages of tasks **running or waiting for CPU, plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D)** on Linux.

Compare to CPU count (`nproc`): load 4 on 8 CPUs ≈ 50% demand; load 16 on 8 ≈ saturated. High load with idle CPU → likely I/O (D state).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `uptime` → load 12.3, 11.8, 6.1 on 4 CPUs: saturation started ~10 min ago and is rising (1-min > 15-min).

bands.text: Busy: close to full CPU demand.
Saturated: tasks are queueing. Check whether they're R (CPU) or D (I/O).
Severe saturation: expect latency; act now (find culprit, shed load).

quiz.why: Correct answer: Runnable tasks and D-state (uninterruptible) tasks.
Correct answer: About 3× more demand than CPUs.
Correct answer: Load is rising recently.

lessons.title: Lab: CPU — top and vmstat

scenes.text: app16 slow; top shows 100% CPU.
Is it user, system, iowait or steal?

steps.title: CPU breakdown
steps.body:
top header `%Cpu(s): us sy ni id wa hi si st`:
- **us** user code, **sy** kernel, **wa** waiting on I/O (CPU idle!), **st** stolen by hypervisor (noisy neighbour)
- `vmstat 1 5`: **r** run queue, **b** blocked (D), **si/so** swap in/out, **wa**
- In top: `1` per-CPU, `P` sort CPU, `M` sort memory, `H` threads

steps.title: Readings
steps.body:
- us 92% → app code busy (profile/scale)
- sy 40% → syscalls/contention
- wa 60% → disks slow
- st 25% → VM starved: talk to virtualisation team

steps.title: Per-process
steps.body: `pidstat 1 5` (sysstat) shows per-process CPU over time.

activity.prompt: Diagnose the slow server: check vmstat, look at the top header, then find the top CPU process.

responses.out:

  PID USER  PR NI   VIRT   RES  SHR S  %CPU %MEM  TIME+ COMMAND

activity.hint: st 25% = hypervisor steal: the VM isn't getting its CPU.

quiz.why: Correct answer: The hypervisor isn't giving the VM enough CPU time.
Correct answer: CPUs idle waiting on I/O.

lessons.title: Lab: Memory — free, page cache and OOM

scenes.text: A manager panics: free shows 200 MB free on a 32 GB server.
Linux uses spare RAM as cache — 'available' is what matters.

steps.title: Reading free -h
steps.body:
- **free**: truly unused
- **buff/cache**: page cache, reclaimable mostly
- **available**: estimate of memory available for new apps without swapping ← use this
- Real pressure signs: low available, swap si/so > 0 continuously, OOM kills, major page faults

steps.title: OOM
steps.body: `journalctl -k | grep -i 'out of memory'` → `Out of memory: Killed process 2210 (java) … anon-rss:7.4GB`. Find the leak or set limits (MemoryMax=, JVM -Xmx).

steps.title: Don't drop caches as a fix
steps.body: `echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches` only hides symptoms and hurts performance.

lessons.title: Lab: Disk I/O — iostat and iotop

scenes.text: db13: load 18, CPU idle 70%, queries slow.
Classic I/O saturation.

steps.title: iostat -xz 1
steps.body:
- **r/s w/s** IOPS
- **r_await w_await** average ms per request (latency)
- **aqu-sz** average queue size
- **%util** busy time (for SSD/arrays, 100% doesn't always mean maxed — look at await)
- `iotop -o` per-process I/O; `pidstat -d 1`

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: sdb: w_await 180 ms, aqu-sz 32, %util 100 → saturated or degraded storage. Find the writer (iotop) and check the array/SAN.

steps.title: Baselines
steps.body: SSD latency is typically well under a few ms; sustained tens/hundreds of ms signals trouble.

steps.title: sar

- `sar -r` memory, `sar -B` paging, `sar -d -p` disks, `sar -n DEV` network, `sar -q` load/run queue
- Older days: `sar -f /var/log/sa/sa25` (path varies: /var/log/sysstat on Debian)

steps.title: Story
steps.body: sar -q shows load from 1 → 14 at 01:05; sar -d shows sdb await 200 ms; cron shows a new 01:00 full reindex job. Cause found.

steps.title: RCA format
steps.body: Impact, timeline, root cause, contributing factors, corrective & preventive actions.

courses.title: Containers for Linux admins: Podman & Docker
courses.summary: What containers really are (namespaces, cgroups, images, layers) and how to run them like an admin: Podman/Docker CLI, ports and volumes, logs, rootless containers with SELinux, and systemd integration. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can explain containers vs VMs in kernel terms
Learners can run, inspect, log and stop containers
Learners can persist data with volumes and publish ports
Learners can run a container as a systemd service (Quadlet)

lessons.title: Containers are Linux processes

scenes.text: Devs ship everything as containers; ops must run them.
Underneath: namespaces + cgroups + an image filesystem.

steps.title: Kernel features
steps.body:
- **Namespaces** isolate views: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user
- **cgroups** limit/account CPU, memory, I/O
- **Image**: layered read-only filesystem (OCI format) + a thin writable layer
- Container = process(es) with those settings; shares the host kernel
- VM = full guest kernel on a hypervisor

steps.title: See it
steps.body: `podman run -d --name web nginx` → `ps -ef | grep nginx` on the host shows the processes; `lsns` lists namespaces.

steps.title: Podman vs Docker
steps.body: Podman is daemonless and rootless-friendly (default on RHEL); CLI is largely Docker-compatible (`alias docker=podman`).

activity.prompt: Container or virtual machine?

items.text: Starts in well under a second typically
Can run a different OS family (e.g. Windows on Linux host)

quiz.q: A Linux container on a Linux host uses…

lessons.title: Lab: Run, inspect and log a container

scenes.text: Tanya runs nginx in a container and publishes it.
Then inspects it like any process.

steps.title: CLI
steps.body:
- `podman pull docker.io/library/nginx:1.27`
- `podman run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27`
- `podman ps`, `podman logs -f web`, `podman exec -it web sh`
- `podman inspect web`, `podman stats`
- `podman stop web && podman rm web`
- Use fully-qualified image names and pinned tags (avoid :latest in prod)

steps.title: Port mapping
steps.body: `-p 8080:80` = host 8080 → container 80. `curl localhost:8080`.

steps.title: Ephemeral
steps.body: Anything written inside the container's layer disappears with `rm`. Use volumes for data.

lessons.title: Lab: Volumes, SELinux and rootless

scenes.text: A dev's database container was recreated — and the data was gone.
Volumes, with the right SELinux label.

steps.title: Persistence
steps.body:
- Named volume: `podman volume create pgdata`; `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`
- Bind mount: `-v /srv/site:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro,Z`
- **:Z** relabels for this container only (private), **:z** shared between containers (SELinux hosts)
- Rootless: run as normal user; ports < 1024 need extra config; storage under `~/.local/share/containers`

steps.title: Permission denied in container
steps.body: Bind mount without :Z on an SELinux host → app gets 'Permission denied' reading files. Add `:Z` (never on system dirs like /home or /usr).

steps.title: Never :Z a system directory
steps.body: Relabelling /etc or /home for a container breaks the host.

activity.prompt: As rootless user, serve /home/tanya/site via nginx read-only with the correct SELinux label, then check the label and test.

options: Relabels content private to that container
quiz.why: Correct answer: Relabels content private to that container.

options: Managed by the engine, survives container removal
quiz.why: Correct answer: Managed by the engine, survives container removal.

quiz.q: Rootless containers can't bind port 80 by default because…
quiz.why: Correct answer: Unprivileged users can't bind ports < 1024 (net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start).
Correct answer: System directories like /home or /etc.

lessons.title: Lab: Run a container as a systemd service (Quadlet)

scenes.text: The status page container must start at boot and restart on failure.
Quadlet turns a .container file into a systemd unit.

steps.title: Quadlet
steps.body:
`/etc/containers/systemd/status.container` (rootful) or `~/.config/containers/systemd/` (rootless):
```
[Unit]
Description=Status page

[Container]
Image=docker.io/library/nginx:1.27
PublishPort=8082:80
Volume=/srv/status:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro,Z

[Service]
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```
Then `systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl start status` (generated unit = status.service).

steps.title: Older way

lessons.title: Units, targets and the boot process

scenes.text: Sana restarted nginx, rebooted the VM, and nginx was down again.

steps.title: Unit types
steps.body:
- `.service` daemons, `.socket` socket activation, `.timer` schedules, `.mount`/`.automount`, `.target` groups of units, `.path` file watchers
- Vendor units: `/usr/lib/systemd/system`; admin units/overrides: `/etc/systemd/system` (wins)
- Targets: `multi-user.target` (text, servers), `graphical.target`, `rescue.target`, `emergency.target`

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `systemctl get-default` → multi-user.target. `systemctl set-default graphical.target` changes the boot target. `systemctl isolate rescue.target` switches now.

steps.title: start vs enable
steps.body: `start` = now; `enable` = create symlinks so it starts at boot; `enable --now` does both. `mask` links to /dev/null so nothing can start it.

lessons.title: Lab: Write a custom service unit

scenes.text: Developers hand Sana a Flask app started with 'python3 app.py' in tmux.
She turns it into a supervised systemd service with restarts and a dedicated user.

steps.title: Minimal unit
steps.body:
```
[Unit]
Description=Orders API
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=orders
WorkingDirectory=/opt/orders
ExecStart=/opt/orders/venv/bin/python app.py
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
Environment=PORT=8081

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

steps.title: Hardening extras
steps.body: `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `ProtectSystem=full`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, `UMask=0027`, `MemoryMax=512M`. `systemd-analyze security orders` scores exposure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Relative path in ExecStart (must be absolute)
- Forgetting daemon-reload
- Type=simple program that forks into background → systemd thinks it died; use Type=forking or run in foreground.

steps.title: Drop-ins
steps.body:

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone · Journal forensics after a crash

scenes.text: db02 rebooted unexpectedly at 03:12. Was it the kernel, power, or a person?

steps.title: journalctl filters
steps.body:
- `--list-boots`, `-b -1` previous boot
- `-p err` priority err and above (emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug)
- `--since '2026-11-26 02:50' --until '03:15'`
- `-k` kernel messages, `-f` follow, `-o json-pretty`
- Persistence: `Storage=persistent` in /etc/systemd/journald.conf or create /var/log/journal

steps.title: Clues
steps.body: Kernel OOM: `Out of memory: Killed process`. Human: `systemd-logind: System is rebooting` + sudo entry. Hardware/power: previous boot log simply stops with no shutdown messages.

steps.title: Disk use
steps.body: `journalctl --disk-usage`; trim with `--vacuum-size=500M` or `SystemMaxUse=`.

lessons.title: Package families and how they work

scenes.text: Rohit's team runs Rocky Linux for apps and Ubuntu for CI runners.

steps.title: Layers
steps.body:
| Task | RHEL family | Debian family |
- Low-level: `rpm` / `dpkg` (one local package, no dependency solving)
- High-level: `dnf` (yum) / `apt` (dependency solving, repos)
- Repo config: `/etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo` / `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/*` (newer Ubuntu: `.sources` files)
- Refresh metadata: dnf does it automatically / `apt update` required before install

steps.title: Same task both ways
steps.body:
- Install: `dnf install nginx` / `apt install nginx`
- Search: `dnf search nginx` / `apt search nginx`
- Info: `dnf info nginx` / `apt show nginx`
- Remove: `dnf remove x` / `apt remove x` (`apt purge` also removes config)
- Installed list: `rpm -qa` / `dpkg -l`

steps.title: Mixing tools
steps.body: Don't install random .rpm/.deb files with rpm -i/dpkg -i when a repo exists — you lose dependency handling and updates.

steps.title: Trust

baseurl=https://repo.contoso.local/el9/$basearch/

courses.summary: Automate recurring work reliably: crontab syntax, environment pitfalls, one-off at jobs, systemd timers with OnCalendar and Persistent, and logging/alerting for scheduled jobs. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can write and read crontab lines confidently

lessons.title: Lab: Crontab syntax drills

story.title: The report that ran every minute

scenes.text: Someone wrote '* 2 * * *' meaning 2 a.m. — it ran 60 times between 02:00 and 02:59.
Five fields, carefully.

steps.title: Five fields
steps.body:
`minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week command`

- `30 2 * * *` 02:30 daily
- `*/15 * * * *` every 15 minutes
- `0 9 * * 1-5` 09:00 Mon–Fri
- `0 0 1 * *` midnight on the 1st
- `@reboot`, `@daily` shortcuts
- `crontab -e` edit, `-l` list, `-u user` as root; system jobs in `/etc/cron.d/` include a **user** field

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. 'At 23:45 every Sunday' → `45 23 * * 0`.
2. 'Every 6 hours on the hour' → `0 */6 * * *` (00,06,12,18).
3. `0 2 * * *` — the fix for the 60-runs bug.

steps.title: DOM + DOW
steps.body: If both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, cron runs when **either** matches. `0 0 1 * 1` = 1st of month OR every Monday.

lessons.title: Lab: Make a cron job that actually works

scenes.text: Pooja's backup script runs fine by hand but does nothing in cron.
Cron has a tiny PATH and no terminal.

steps.title: Cron pitfalls
steps.body:
- Minimal environment: PATH often `/usr/bin:/bin` → use absolute paths or set `PATH=` in the crontab
- `%` is special in crontab (newline) → escape as `\%` e.g. `date +\%F`
- Output is mailed to the owner or lost → redirect `>> /var/log/job.log 2>&1`
- Logs of cron itself: `journalctl -u crond` (RHEL) / `-u cron` (Debian)

steps.title: Good line
steps.body:
`15 1 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1`

Prevent overlaps: `flock -n /run/backup.lock /usr/local/bin/backup.sh`.

steps.title: Test in cron's environment
steps.body: `env -i /bin/sh -c '/usr/local/bin/backup.sh'` approximates the bare environment.

scenes.text: A laptop-class edge box is off at 02:00 and misses its cleanup every night.
A timer with Persistent=true catches up at boot.

steps.title: Timer + service pair
steps.body:
`cleanup.service` (Type=oneshot, ExecStart=…) and `cleanup.timer`:
```
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00
Persistent=true
RandomizedDelaySec=10min

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```
- Enable the **timer**: `systemctl enable --now cleanup.timer`
- `systemctl list-timers` next/last run
- `systemd-analyze calendar 'Mon..Fri 18:00'` validates expressions

steps.title: OnCalendar examples
steps.body:
- `daily` = `*-*-* 00:00:00`
- `Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00`
- `*-*-01 03:00` 1st of month
- `*:0/15` every 15 minutes
- Monotonic: `OnBootSec=5min`, `OnUnitActiveSec=1h`

steps.title: Why timers
steps.body: Logs in the journal per run, dependencies, resource controls, catch-up with Persistent, no overlap (the service won't start twice while active).

lessons.title: Lab: Generate and deploy a key pair

scenes.text: Security mandates key-only SSH to all prod hosts by Friday.
Tanvi creates an ed25519 key and deploys it.

steps.title: Keys
steps.body:
- `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'tanvi@laptop'` → `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (private, keep secret, passphrase!) and `.pub` (public)
- `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub tanvi@web01` appends to remote `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`
- Permissions matter: `~/.ssh` 700, `authorized_keys` 600 (sshd StrictModes rejects loose perms)

steps.title: Fingerprints
steps.body: `ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` → `256 SHA256:Vq3… tanvi@laptop (ED25519)`. On first connect compare the host key fingerprint with one published by the server admin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Copying the private key to servers
- No passphrase on a laptop key
- Ignoring 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED' (could be MITM — verify before `ssh-keygen -R host`)

lessons.title: Lab: Harden sshd

scenes.text: Pen-test report: root login allowed, password auth on, no login rate limits.
Tanvi hardens sshd without locking herself out.

steps.title: Key settings
steps.body:
In `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` or a drop-in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-hardening.conf`:
- `PermitRootLogin no`
- `PasswordAuthentication no` (only after keys work!)
- `AllowGroups sshusers`
- `MaxAuthTries 3`, `LoginGraceTime 30`
- Note: the **first** occurrence of a keyword wins in sshd_config; drop-ins are Included near the top on modern distros

steps.title: Safe procedure
steps.body:
1. Keep your current session open
2. Edit, `sshd -t`
3. `systemctl reload sshd`
4. Test a **new** session from another terminal
5. Only then close the old one

steps.title: Lockout
steps.body: Disabling passwords before your key works, or AllowGroups without adding yourself, = lockout → console access needed.

scenes.text: Prod hosts in 10.40.0.0/16 are reachable only via bastion.contoso.local.

steps.title: ~/.ssh/config
steps.body:
```
Host bastion
  HostName bastion.contoso.local
  User tanvi

Host db01
  HostName 10.40.2.11
  User tanvi
  ProxyJump bastion
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```
- `ssh -J bastion tanvi@10.40.2.11` one-off
- `ssh-add` loads key into agent

steps.title: Agent forwarding risk
steps.body: `ForwardAgent yes` lets root on the intermediate host use your agent. Prefer ProxyJump, which keeps keys local.

steps.title: Debugging
steps.body: `ssh -vvv db01` shows which keys are tried and where it fails. `ssh -G db01` prints the resolved client config.

courses.summary: Stop disabling SELinux: understand modes, contexts and types, diagnose AVC denials, fix file contexts with semanage/restorecon, use booleans and port labels. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can read SELinux mode and contexts
Learners can find and interpret AVC denials

lessons.title: Modes, contexts and type enforcement

scenes.text: A forum post tells Zoya to disable SELinux to fix a 403.
Her senior says: 'Understand the label, fix the label.'

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- Modes: **enforcing** (deny + log), **permissive** (log only), **disabled**
- `getenforce`, `setenforce 0|1` (runtime), `/etc/selinux/config` (boot)
- Every process and file has a context `user:role:type:level`, e.g. `system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0`
- **Type enforcement**: policy says which process types (domains like `httpd_t`) may access which file/port types

steps.title: See labels
steps.body: `ls -Z /var/www/html` → `httpd_sys_content_t`. `ps -eZ | grep httpd` → `system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0`. Files in /home are `user_home_t` — httpd_t can't read them.

steps.title: Why not disable
steps.body: SELinux contains a compromised service. Disabling it removes a major barrier. Switching from disabled back to enforcing needs a full relabel.

pairs: Type of files in home dirs

lessons.title: Lab: Diagnose an AVC denial

scenes.text: Zoya moved a site from /home/zoya/site to /var/www/shop with mv. Apache returns 403.
Permissions look fine. The audit log says otherwise.

steps.title: Finding denials
steps.body:
- `ausearch -m AVC -ts recent`
- `journalctl -t setroubleshoot` (if setroubleshoot installed) — plain-English advice
- `sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log`
- Raw: `grep denied /var/log/audit/audit.log`

steps.title: Reading one
steps.body:
`avc: denied { read } for pid=2211 comm="httpd" name="index.html" scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 tclass=file permissive=0`

→ httpd_t tried to read a user_home_t file. **mv keeps the old label**; cp creates a new label from the destination.

steps.title: Quick fix vs right fix
steps.body: `restorecon -Rv /var/www/shop` resets labels to the policy default for that path — correct here because /var/www already maps to httpd_sys_content_t.

activity.prompt: Apache returns 403 for /var/www/shop. Check SELinux mode, find the AVC denial, look at the labels, restore them and retest.

Relabeled /var/www/shop/index.html from unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0
Relabeled /var/www/shop/css from unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 to unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0

quiz.why: Correct answer: mv keeps the original SELinux label.

quiz.why: Correct answer: The policy default for that path.

lessons.title: Lab: Custom paths with semanage fcontext

scenes.text: The web team wants the site on a big disk at /srv/web.
There's no default rule for /srv/web, so Zoya adds one.

steps.title: Persistent labelling
steps.body:
- `semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?'` adds a rule
- `restorecon -Rv /srv/web` applies it
- `semanage fcontext -l | grep srv/web` view
- `chcon -t …` is **temporary**: a relabel or restorecon reverts it
- Writable dirs for apps: `httpd_sys_rw_content_t`

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Uploads dir needs writes: `semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_rw_content_t '/srv/web/uploads(/.*)?'` then restorecon.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the regex `(/.*)?` labels only the directory itself, not its contents.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone · Fix a service without disabling SELinux

scenes.text: INC0077312: After moving Nextcloud data to /data/nc, uploads fail. A colleague suggests disabling SELinux.
Zoya fixes it properly and documents.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Reproduce, `ausearch -m AVC -ts recent`
2. Identify domain/target types
3. Prefer: correct label (fcontext) > boolean > port label > custom module (`audit2allow`) as last resort, reviewed
4. Verify enforcing still on

steps.title: audit2allow caution
steps.body: `audit2allow -M mymod` can grant far more than needed. Review the .te file; usually a label or boolean is the real fix.

steps.title: Communicate
steps.body: Explain in the ticket why disabling was rejected and what was changed.

ticket.short: File uploads failing after storage move
ticket.description: We moved data to the new disk /data/nc yesterday and now uploads give 'internal server error'. Downloads of old files also fail sometimes. Someone said SELinux is the problem, can you just turn it off?

investigate.label: ausearch -m AVC -ts today
investigate.reveal: avc: denied { write } for comm="php-fpm" name="nc" scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=system_u:object_r:default_t:s0 tclass=dir

options: SELinux is buggy and must be disabled
New path /data/nc has default_t label; php-fpm (httpd_t) can't write — needs httpd_sys_rw_content_t
diagnosis.why: The AVC shows httpd_t denied write on default_t; no fcontext rule exists for the new path.

resolution: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_rw_content_t '/data/nc(/.*)?'
restorecon -Rv /data/nc
Test upload and download
Confirm getenforce = Enforcing
Update ticket explaining why SELinux stays on

closure.model: Root cause: after migrating data to /data/nc the directory kept default_t, so php-fpm (httpd_t) was denied write (AVC). Fix: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_rw_content_t '/data/nc(/.*)?' + restorecon -Rv. Verified upload/download OK. SELinux remains Enforcing; disabling was not required.

lessons.title: Where logs live

scenes.text: New joiner Dev is asked 'check the logs' with no further hints.
Mapping symptoms to log files saves hours.

steps.title: Map
steps.body:
- journald: everything from systemd units (`journalctl`)
- `/var/log/messages` (RHEL) or `/var/log/syslog` (Debian) — general syslog
- `/var/log/secure` (RHEL) / `/var/log/auth.log` (Debian) — authentication, sudo
- `/var/log/audit/audit.log` — auditd/SELinux
- `/var/log/dnf.log` / `/var/log/apt/history.log` — package changes
- App logs: `/var/log/nginx/`, `/var/log/mariadb/`, app-specific dirs
- `dmesg` / `journalctl -k` — kernel ring buffer (disks, OOM, NIC)

steps.title: Symptom → log
steps.body: 'Who ran sudo rm last night?' → secure/auth.log. 'Disk errors?' → `journalctl -k | grep -i 'I/O error'`. 'When was openssl updated?' → dnf.log / apt history.

steps.title: Timestamps & time zones
steps.body: Correlate in one time zone; check `timedatectl` and that NTP (chronyd) is synced — skewed clocks wreck timelines.

steps.title: logrotate rule
steps.body:
`/etc/logrotate.d/orders`:
```
/var/log/orders/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 orders orders
    postrotate
        systemctl kill -s HUP orders.service
    endscript
}
```
- Runs daily via a systemd timer (logrotate.timer) or cron.daily
- `copytruncate` for apps that can't reopen logs (small risk of losing lines)

4. Separate facts from hypotheses; preserve evidence (copy logs, hashes)

lessons.title: Block devices and naming

scenes.text: The cloud team attached a new disk to db04. Where is it?
Linux names disks sda, vda, nvme0n1… and the name isn't guaranteed stable.

steps.title: Naming
steps.body:
- SCSI/SATA/virtio-scsi: `/dev/sda`, partitions `/dev/sda1`
- virtio-blk: `/dev/vda`
- NVMe: `/dev/nvme0n1`, partitions `/dev/nvme0n1p1`
- Stable names: `/dev/disk/by-uuid/`, `by-id/`, `by-path/`
- Tools: `lsblk -f`, `blkid`, `fdisk -l`, `dmesg | tail`

steps.title: GPT vs MBR
steps.body:
- **MBR**: max 2 TiB per disk (with 512-byte sectors), 4 primary partitions (or extended)
- **GPT**: huge disks, 128 partitions by default, backup header at the end, required for UEFI boot

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `lsblk` shows `sdb 8:16 0 100G 0 disk` with no children → new, unpartitioned. Rescan after hot-add if needed: `echo '- - -' > /sys/class/scsi_host/host0/scan`.

scenes.text: Ishaan must create one GPT partition on /dev/sdb, format it XFS and mount it at /data.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. `lsblk` — confirm the target is the empty disk
2. `parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel gpt mkpart data xfs 1MiB 100%`
3. `mkfs.xfs -L data /dev/sdb1`
4. `mkdir /data && mount /dev/sdb1 /data`
5. `df -h /data`

steps.title: ext4 alternative
steps.body: `mkfs.ext4 -L data /dev/sdb1`. ext4 can shrink (offline); XFS cannot shrink at all.

steps.title: Alignment & mistakes
steps.body: Start at 1MiB for alignment. Never run mkfs on a mounted or wrong device — `lsblk` first, every time.

steps.body:

2. Grow partition: `growpart /dev/sdb 1` (cloud-utils-growpart) or parted `resizepart`
3. Grow filesystem: XFS `xfs_growfs /data` (mount point); ext4 `resize2fs /dev/sdb1`

steps.title: Check each layer
steps.body: `lsblk` (disk & part size) → `df -h` (filesystem size). If lsblk shows 200G disk but 100G partition, step 2 is missing.

scenes.text: After a SAN hiccup, app05's /data remounted read-only.

steps.title: Tools
steps.body:
- Kernel: `dmesg | grep -iE 'error|xfs|ext4'`
- ext4: `e2fsck -f /dev/sdX1` (unmounted)
- XFS: `xfs_repair /dev/sdX1` (unmounted); `xfs_repair -n` no-modify check
- If XFS says log is dirty: mount once to replay; `-L` zeroes the log (data loss risk) — last resort

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: Stop app → `umount /data` → `xfs_repair -n /dev/sdc1` → `xfs_repair /dev/sdc1` → mount → check app.

steps.title: Never fsck a mounted filesystem
steps.body: Repairing a mounted fs can corrupt it further. Root fs: boot rescue mode.

lessons.title: LVM concepts

scenes.text: Fixed partitions keep filling. Lakshmi wants volumes she can grow without downtime.
LVM pools disks into volume groups.

steps.title: Layers
steps.body:
- **PV** physical volume: a disk or partition (`pvcreate`)
- **VG** volume group: pool of PVs, carved into **extents** (default 4 MiB)
- **LV** logical volume: block device from VG extents → `/dev/vg/lv` = `/dev/mapper/vg-lv`
- Views: `pvs`, `vgs`, `lvs` (short), `pvdisplay`… (long)

steps.title: Extent maths
steps.body: VG of 2 × 50 GiB PVs with 4 MiB extents ≈ 25,598 extents (some space used for metadata). An LV of 10 GiB = 2,560 extents.

steps.title: Leave free space
steps.body: Keep some VG space free for snapshots and emergencies.

mount /dev/vgdata/lvweb /srv/web

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Snapshot workflow
steps.body:
1. `lvcreate -s -n site_snap -L 5G /dev/vgweb/lvsite` (5G for changes during backup)
2. Mount read-only: XFS needs `-o ro,nouuid` (duplicate UUID)
3. Back up from the mount (tar/rsync)
4. `umount`, `lvremove -y /dev/vgweb/site_snap`

Watch `lvs` Data% — at 100% the snapshot becomes invalid.

steps.title: Commands
steps.body: `mount -o ro,nouuid /dev/vgweb/site_snap /mnt/snap && tar czf /backup/site-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /mnt/snap .`

steps.title: Snapshots aren't backups
steps.body: They live on the same disks. Copy data off, then remove the snapshot (they also slow writes).

lessons.title: Lab: fstab anatomy and testing

story.title: The server that didn't come back

scenes.text: After a reboot app06 dropped to emergency mode: a typo in fstab.
Six fields, and a test before every reboot.

steps.title: Fields
steps.body:
`UUID=5f1c…  /data  xfs  defaults,noatime  0 0`

1. device (UUID=, LABEL=, /dev/mapper/…)
2. mount point
3. type
4. options
5. dump (0)
6. fsck order (root 1, others 2 for ext4; 0 for XFS)

scenes.text: batch01 has 8 GB RAM, no swap, and the OOM killer strikes during reports.

steps.title: Swap
steps.body:
File:
```
dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=4096
chmod 600 /swapfile
mkswap /swapfile
swapon /swapfile
```
fstab: `/swapfile none swap defaults 0 0`. LV: `lvcreate -L 4G -n swap2 rhel; mkswap; swapon`.

`swapon --show`, `free -h`; `vm.swappiness` tunes eagerness.

steps.title: Notes
steps.body: `fallocate` swap files work on ext4/XFS on modern kernels, but dd is universally safe. Swap is a buffer, not a fix for chronic memory shortage.

courses.title: Disk full: find and free space safely
courses.summary: The most common Linux ticket. Diagnose with df, du, ncdu and lsof, handle inode exhaustion and deleted-but-open files, clean logs/journals/caches safely and prevent recurrence. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can find what's using space quickly
Learners can diagnose inode exhaustion
Learners can free space held by deleted-open files
Learners can choose safe clean-ups and prevent recurrence

lessons.title: Lab: df and du like a pro

scenes.text: Alert: web09 root filesystem 100%. Nginx can't write and logins are slow.
Kabir starts with df then drills down with du.

steps.title: Drill-down
steps.body:
- `df -h` which filesystem is full; `df -i` inodes
- `du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h` biggest top-level dirs on that filesystem only (-x)
- Repeat one level deeper
- `find / -xdev -type f -size +1G -exec ls -lh {} +`
- `ncdu -x /` interactive (if installed)

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `du -xh -d1 /var | sort -h` → `31G /var/log`. `du -h -d1 /var/log | sort -h` → `29G /var/log/app`. Culprit: un-rotated debug log.

steps.title: Don't rm blindly
steps.body: Deleting files under /var/lib (databases, packages) can break the system. Know what a file is first.

lessons.title: Lab: Deleted but still open

scenes.text: Kabir deleted a 20 GB log, but df still says 100%.
A process still holds the file open.

steps.title: Why
steps.body:
Deleting removes the name; blocks are freed only when the last open file descriptor closes.

- `lsof +L1` or `lsof -nP | grep '(deleted)'`
- Options: restart/reload the process, or truncate via its fd: `: > /proc/PID/fd/N`

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `lsof +L1` → `java 4412 app 12w REG 253,0 21474836480 0 1311 /var/log/app/debug.log (deleted)`. `: > /proc/4412/fd/12` frees 20 GB immediately.

steps.title: Better: truncate instead of rm
steps.body: For a live log, `truncate -s 0 file` or `: > file` empties it without orphaning the inode.

lessons.title: Lab: Inodes exhausted

scenes.text: mail01 refuses to write: No space left on device — yet df -h shows 60% free.
Millions of tiny files used every inode.

steps.title: Inodes
steps.body:
Each file uses one inode. ext4 sets the count at mkfs time; XFS allocates dynamically (but can still run out).

- `df -i` → IUse% 100%
- Find dirs with most files: `find / -xdev -printf '%h\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`
- Typical culprits: session files, mail queues, cache dirs

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: `/var/lib/php/session` with 4.1 M files. Clean with `find /var/lib/php/session -type f -mmin +1440 -delete` and fix PHP session GC.

steps.title: rm * fails
steps.body: 'Argument list too long' — use find -delete.

lessons.title: Lab: Safe clean-up toolkit

scenes.text: Kabir needs quick wins without breaking anything.
Known-safe cleanups first.

steps.title: Usually safe (verify policy)
steps.body:
- Journal: `journalctl --vacuum-size=500M` or `--vacuum-time=14d`
- Package caches: `dnf clean all` / `apt clean`
- Old kernels: `dnf remove --oldinstallonly` (keep ≥2) / `apt autoremove`
- Rotated logs `*.gz` per retention policy
- Container images: `podman image prune` / `docker system prune` (check!)
- Core dumps: `coredumpctl list`, `/var/lib/systemd/coredump`

steps.title: Never
steps.body:
- `rm -rf /var/lib/mysql/*` or database files to 'make space'
- delete `/var/lib/rpm` or `/var/lib/dpkg`
- delete files under /proc or /sys

steps.title: Quick win
steps.body: `journalctl --disk-usage` → 4.0G. `journalctl --vacuum-size=500M` → 'Vacuuming done, freed 3.5G'.
